title: Life Skills Shorts · Episode 3
chapters: Making an insurance claim that sticks
When someone dies: the practical steps

units.t: Life Skills Shorts. Episode three.
In this episode: Making an insurance claim that sticks, Reading a map and compass, When someone dies: the practical steps and Private health insurance, decoded.
Part one. Making an insurance claim that sticks.
You pay premiums for years hoping you never need them.
When something finally goes wrong, how you handle the first days of a claim can make a real difference to the outcome.
Prepare before disaster.
The best time to prepare for a claim is a quiet weekday, long before a storm or break-in.
Download your product disclosure statement, the long document that sets out what your policy covers, and read the sections on exclusions and how claims work.
Check your sum insured for home and contents.
Underinsurance is common, because people guess the value of their belongings and fall well short.
Many insurers offer online calculators for rebuilding or replacement costs.
Film each room and store the video in the cloud, along with receipts for expensive items.
Note your excess, the amount you pay towards each claim.
This is general information, not advice; read your own policy.
Make safe, then document.
Imagine coming home to water pouring through the ceiling.
Safety comes first: turn off water or power if it is safe, and call emergency services if anyone is in danger.
Policies generally expect reasonable steps to prevent further damage, such as a tarp or an emergency plumber, and those costs are often covered.
Before you throw anything away, photograph and film the damage, including serial numbers and brand labels.
Keep damaged items until the insurer says you may dispose of them.
After a car crash, exchange names, contact details, registrations and insurer details, photograph the scene, collect witness details and don't admit fault, as that is for insurers to work out.
Report theft to police and record the event number.
Lodge and keep a log.
Contact your insurer as soon as practical, through their app, website or claims line.
Delays can complicate a claim, especially if damage worsens.
You will receive a claim number; write it on every document and email.
Start a simple claim log on paper or in a notes app.
Record the date and time of every call, who you spoke to and what was agreed.
Follow up important calls with a short email confirming what was said.
Be honest and accurate in everything you tell the insurer.
Exaggerating a claim, even slightly, can give the insurer grounds to refuse it or cancel your policy, and it can have serious legal consequences.
Assessors and settlement.
For larger claims, the insurer may send an assessor or ask for quotes from builders.
You can generally supply your own quotes, and it is reasonable to ask for a copy of the assessor's report.
Insurers may offer to manage repairs through their own builders, or offer a cash settlement.
Cash can seem attractive, but check that it would cover the real cost of fixing the damage with a licensed tradesperson.
Once you accept it, the insurer usually has no further responsibility for the repairs.
Ask how the figure was calculated.
Keep receipts for temporary accommodation and emergency costs, as some policies cover these up to a limit.
Decisions and disputes.
Insurers that subscribe to the General Insurance Code of Practice commit to keeping you updated, deciding within set timeframes and explaining their reasons.
If your claim is denied, ask in writing for the decision, the policy wording relied on and any reports used.
Sometimes a refusal rests on a misunderstanding that extra evidence, like a receipt or tradesperson's report, can fix.
If you still disagree, make a formal written complaint, use the word 'complaint', and say what outcome you want.
Most complaints should get a response within about 30 calendar days.
If you are unhappy or hear nothing, lodge a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority at afca.
org.
au.
It is free for consumers and independent of insurers, and its decisions can bind the insurer.
The key idea: Know your policy, sum insured and excess before you need to claim, because underinsurance is common.
Part two. Reading a map and compass.
Phones die, satellites drop out and screens are hard to read in the rain.
A paper map and a compass need no battery, and the skills to use them are surprisingly learnable.
Paper and scale.
Phone navigation is brilliant until the battery goes flat in the cold, the screen cracks or you lose signal in a deep valley.
Bushwalking clubs and search and rescue groups in Australia still advise carrying a paper map and compass, and knowing how to use them, as a backup.
Navigating with a map also makes you read the land and notice ridges and creeks.
People following a blue dot often have little idea of their surroundings.
Walking maps are usually topographic, with scales such as 1:25,000 or 1:50,000.
On a 1:25,000 map, one centimetre is 250 metres; on a 1:50,000 map, 500 metres.
The larger the second number, the more ground the map covers and the less detail.
Map distance is flat, so a steep kilometre takes longer than a level one.
Contours and grid references.
Each contour line joins points of the same height, and the contour interval is in the legend.
Close lines mean steep ground; wide spacing means gentle ground.
Stacked closed rings mark a hill or peak.
V or U shapes pointing uphill show a valley or gully, often with a creek.
Pointing downhill, they show a spur, a ridge running down from higher ground.
A grid reference describes a location precisely, perhaps to rescuers.
Australian topographic maps use the Map Grid of Australia, with vertical lines called eastings and horizontal lines called northings.
Give the easting first, then the northing: ‘along the corridor, then up the stairs’.
A four-figure reference identifies a grid square, usually one kilometre across.
Six figures estimate tenths within it, to about 100 metres.
Norths and bearings.
True north is the geographic North Pole.
Grid north follows the map's vertical grid lines and is very close to true north.
Magnetic north is where your compass points.
The difference is magnetic declination.
In Australia it ranges from near zero in parts of Western Australia to over ten degrees east in the south-east.
Maps print the declination.
A ten-degree error over five kilometres puts you almost a kilometre off course.
To take a bearing, lay a baseplate compass's edge on the map joining where you are to where you are going, with its arrow pointing to the destination.
Turn the dial until the orienting lines parallel the grid lines, with the orienting arrow to the top of the map.
Read the bearing, then correct for declination: where it is east, subtract it.
Walking on a bearing.
Hold the compass flat with the direction-of-travel arrow pointing ahead.
Turn your whole body until the red, north end of the needle sits inside the orienting arrow, often remembered as ‘red in the shed’.
The arrow now points along your bearing.
Rather than staring at the compass, pick a distinct landmark in that direction, walk to it, then repeat.
Keep the compass away from metal, phones, car bodies and power lines, which can pull the needle.
Another technique is aiming off: when heading for a point on a creek or track, deliberately aim to one side so you know which way to turn on arrival.
A compass for here.
Earth's magnetic field also dips downward at an angle that changes with latitude.
A compass needle is weighted to cancel that dip in the region where it will be used.
A compass balanced for Europe or North America may tilt, drag on its housing and read sluggishly in Australia.
Check it is balanced for the southern hemisphere or Australian zone, or choose a global needle.
Practise somewhere safe and familiar, such as a local park or well-marked track, before relying on your skills in remote country.
And always tell someone your plans and carry an emergency beacon where there is no phone coverage.
The key idea: A paper map and compass never run out of battery, and a map's scale tells you real distances.
Part three. When someone dies: the practical steps.
In the middle of grief come phone calls, forms and decisions nobody prepares you for.
Knowing the order of things can lift some of the weight.
First hours and certification.
If someone dies suddenly or unexpectedly, or you are unsure whether they have died, call Triple Zero, 000, straight away.
Operators will guide you, and paramedics and often police will attend.
If the death was expected, for example someone in palliative care at home, there is no need for an ambulance.
Contact their doctor or palliative care team, who will arrange for the death to be confirmed.
There is generally no requirement to have the body taken away immediately, so you can take time to sit with the person and call family.
Before a funeral, a doctor must complete a medical certificate stating the cause of death.
Sudden, unexpected, violent, accidental or unexplained deaths must be reported to the coroner, who may order a post-mortem or an inquest.
Coronial staff can explain each step.
The funeral and registration.

Most families engage a funeral director, who collects the person, helps arrange the service and usually lodges the details to register the death with the state or territory Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages.
The registry then issues the official death certificate, which differs from the doctor's medical certificate.
You will need it, or certified copies, for banks, super funds and insurers.
Check whether the person left wishes about burial, cremation or music.
A funeral can be religious or secular, large or small.
Funerals can cost many thousands of dollars, and grieving families may overspend out of love or guilt.
Get more than one quote, ask for itemised prices and consider simpler options such as direct cremation followed by a memorial gathering.
A calmer friend can join the meetings.
Telling organisations.

A surprising number of organisations need to be told: Services Australia for Centrelink and Medicare, the Australian Taxation Office, banks, super funds, insurers, employers, utility and phone companies, and more.
The free Australian Death Notification Service, run with the state registries, lets you notify a number of participating organisations in one go once the death is registered.
Keep a list of who you have contacted, when and what they said.
Many banks and large companies have dedicated bereavement teams who can make it gentler.
Redirecting mail and closing unused accounts also helps protect against criminals who misuse the identities of people who have died.
Money and the estate.
If there is a will, the executor it names manages the estate: gathering assets, paying debts and distributing what remains.
If there is no will, a close relative can apply to the court to be appointed administrator.
Until it is clear who has the authority, avoid giving away belongings or money, however obvious the wishes seem.
Some things move outside the estate.
Jointly held bank accounts and property usually pass straight to the surviving owner, and super is paid by the fund's trustee, often following the member's nominations.
Many banks will pay funeral invoices directly from the deceased's account.
A final tax return is often needed, and solicitors and public trustees can help.
Looking after the living.
In the first weeks the to-do list can feel endless, but very little has to happen immediately.
Prioritise the essentials, such as the funeral and anything protecting the estate, and let the rest wait.
Accept practical offers such as cooking, making calls or minding children, and consider putting one organised friend or relative in charge of the paperwork list.
Grief comes in waves and can bring exhaustion, poor sleep and forgetfulness.
Talk with your GP if you are struggling, and know that grief support services exist; Lifeline, 13 11 14, answers any time.
If you are ever worried about your safety or someone else's, call 000.
Being kind to yourself is part of the work.
The key idea: Call 000 for a sudden death, but an expected death needs no rush, and some deaths must go to the coroner.
Part four. Private health insurance, decoded.
Gold, Silver, Bronze, extras, excesses and a mysterious loading after 30.
Here is how private health insurance really works in Australia, so you can decide what you need.
Medicare, choice and tax.
Every Australian resident enrolled in Medicare can be treated free as a public patient in a public hospital.
So why do close to half of Australians hold private hospital cover?
Mostly for choice and timing.
As a private patient you can usually choose your specialist and hospital, and elective surgery such as a knee reconstruction may happen sooner than on a public waiting list.
Tax rules push some people towards cover as well.
The Medicare Levy Surcharge is an extra tax on people above an income threshold who lack appropriate hospital cover.
Separately, the Australian Government Rebate reduces premiums for many people, depending on income and age.
Check current figures at ato.
gov.
au.
Whether cover is worth it depends on your health, age, income and priorities.
This is general information, not financial advice.
Hospital tiers and extras.
Hospital cover pays towards your costs as a private patient, such as accommodation, theatre fees and part of the doctors' fees.
Since 2019, policies sit in four tiers: Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic.
Each must cover a minimum list of clinical categories.
Gold covers all of them, including pregnancy and birth and joint replacements, while a cheap Basic policy may cover very little.
A 'plus' label means extra categories.
Compare the treatments you might realistically need, not just the tier name or price.
Extras pays part of the cost of services outside hospital, such as dental, physio and optical.
Each service has a benefit amount and an annual limit, so you pay the rest.
Add up what you actually spend, then compare it with the premium plus the gaps.
Excess, gaps, waiting periods.
Two policies in the same tier can cost very different amounts because of the excess, the amount you agree to pay upfront if you are admitted to hospital.
A higher excess lowers your premium but raises your bill when you need care.
You may also face a gap, the difference between what a doctor charges and what Medicare and your insurer pay.
Ask your specialist and hospital about likely gaps before treatment, and whether they have an arrangement with your fund.
Waiting periods apply when you first take out cover or upgrade.
They are commonly up to 12 months for pre-existing conditions and pregnancy, and shorter for most other hospital treatment.
Check the specifics before you need them.
Lifetime Health Cover loading.
Lifetime Health Cover encourages people to join earlier.

If you do not hold private hospital cover by 1 July following your 31st birthday, a loading of 2 per cent is added to your hospital premium for every year you are over 30 when you eventually join, up to a maximum of 70 per cent.
Someone first joining at 40 would typically pay around 20 per cent more than someone who joined at 30.
The loading is removed after you have held hospital cover continuously for 10 years.
Some exceptions exist, including for people who arrived in Australia later in life.
Extras-only cover does not count towards avoiding the loading.
Compare and switch.
Insurers have thousands of policies, and names alone tell you little.
The government website privatehealth.
gov.
au, managed by the Commonwealth Ombudsman, lets you compare policies from all registered funds, and every policy has a standard information statement summarising what it covers.
Commercial comparison sites can help, but they may not list every fund.
You can switch funds.
If you move to an equivalent level of hospital cover you generally will not serve the same waiting periods again, though upgrades may attract new ones.
Review your cover each year, especially when life changes, such as planning a family or retiring.
If you have a dispute with your fund, the Commonwealth Ombudsman can help, free of charge.
A tax agent can help you apply the tax rules to your situation.
The key idea: Private cover sits on top of Medicare, mainly for choice and timing, and tax rules also nudge people towards it.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is it worth checking your sum insured before anything goes wrong?
Answer. Underinsurance is common and costly.
Question two. On a 1:50,000 map, what does one centimetre represent?
Answer. 500 metres.
Question three. What should you do first if a death is sudden or unexpected?
Answer. Call Triple Zero, 000,.
Question four. What is a main reason Australians hold private hospital cover?
Answer. Choice of specialist and sooner elective surgery.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
